title: Even with those you dislike
hook: don't let hatred of a people make you unjust, be just (5:8)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the wudu verse. Your line was the washing, written. And a week ends today: peace between two, Isa in the Qur'an's telling, contracts kept, help in goodness, halal, the washing. Now the line that holds them all up. Day three hundred ninety-two.

Scroll through your contacts and one name may make your shoulders rise. A coworker. An ex. The cousin who ruins every holiday. Now someone asks you to describe your last argument with them, and asks for one thing only: be accurate. Not kind. Accurate. Being fair to strangers is easy enough. Fair to the person you can't stand is a different muscle. Fair to a whole group you resent is harder still. Surah five was given to a community that had real opponents, people who had fought them and turned them away from Mecca. Twice in this one surah, the Qur'an stops to say the same hard thing about them.
screen: `THE NAME THAT MAKES YOUR SHOULDERS RISE.` → `NOT KIND. ACCURATE.` → `SAID TWICE IN ONE SURAH.`

segments.voice: The first time is verse two, which you met three days ago: don't let hatred of the people who barred you from the Sacred Mosque push you into wrongdoing. The second is verse eight, today's verse. In Pickthall's words: “let not hatred of any people seduce you that ye deal not justly. Deal justly, that is nearer to your duty.” The Arabic word for that hatred is shana'an, a deep, settled dislike, the kind that has history. And the verse opens by telling believers to be qawwamin, people who stand up and keep standing, as witnesses for Allah in fairness. Now set it beside a verse from a week ago, four, one-thirty-five: stand for justice even against yourselves, your parents, your kin. Commentators have noticed the two verses work as a pair. One guards against bending the truth for the people you love. The other guards against bending it against the people you hate. Love and hate pull the scales in opposite directions, and the Qur'an names both. There's a report in the hadith collections about a companion, Abdullah ibn Rawaha, sent to assess a harvest at Khaybar for people who had been at war with Medina. He told them, more or less: I come from the person I love most, and you are not dear to me, but neither will make me unfair to you. They are said to have answered that this is what holds up the heavens and the earth. And notice the reason the verse gives. Not that your enemy deserves it. That justice is nearer to taqwa, to living aware of God. The fairness is about who you are, not about who they are.
screen: `SHANA'AN — A HATRED WITH HISTORY.` · `QAWWAMIN — THOSE WHO KEEP STANDING.` · `LOVE AND HATE BOTH TIP THE SCALES.` · `NEARER TO TAQWA.` · then, large: `DEAL JUSTLY.`

segments.voice: Bring that person to mind, the one from the phone. Breathe. Now try to say one true thing in their favor. Not a compliment you don't mean. Something accurate: they work hard, they love their kids, they were right about that one thing. If nothing comes, stay with the breath and let the question sit. Then picture one small way to be fair to them today: credit where it's due, their side told straight. The bell holds the time.
Shana'an. The old, settled hatred the Qur'an says must never bend you from being fair, even to the people you resent.
Your line: just, even then. Today, when that person comes up in conversation, tell their side of it straight, once. Day three hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Muslim jurists and teachers cite 5:8 as the ground of fair dealing with opponents, in courts, in trade and in war, and it is often recalled when anger at a whole group of people runs high.

fork.setup: you're Abdullah ibn Rawaha, sent to assess the harvest of people who fought your city. what do you do?
options: estimate fairly, and tell them why.
fork.reveal: the report says he told them neither his love for the Prophet nor his feelings about them would make him unfair, and they said this is what holds up the heavens and the earth.

original.note: Arabic: justice, fairness, setting things level. 5:8 uses the verb: i'dilu, deal justly.

trapdoor: what you thought: be nice to people you don't like.
what it means: be accurate and fair to them, even when there is real history between you.
what a scholar hears: 4:135 and 5:8 mirror each other in wording: one puts justice before witness for Allah, the other witness for Allah before justice, covering bias from love and from hate.
